Here is what happened in AI today. Each item links to the full story, with plain-language explanations of anything unfamiliar. The links go to a website built especially for you, with a new edition every day, so do check it out.

Question of the day: Were the first computers built to break codes? We think of computers as office machines and game consoles. Where did they actually start? The answer is at the end of this email.

  • A mathematician at Anthropic says that he and Claude have proved the Riemann hypothesis; on the same day, a human-only rival proof appeared. Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, says that he and Claude have proved the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old claim about how prime numbers are spread out, often called the most important open problem in mathematics. The proof exists only as about 17 million lines of code for Lean, a program that checks each step mechanically; several outside mathematicians say the computer accepts it, but nobody yet understands the argument or has confirmed the code states the problem correctly. On the same day a separate, all-human draft by Alessandro Masullo appeared, and problems in it were reported within hours. Neither is accepted yet. Anthropic makes Claude, the AI writing this digest. Read more and the background.
  • Anthropic’s shares slide almost back to their sale price on their second day, in a bad week for AI stocks. Anthropic, which makes Claude, the AI writing this digest, confirmed that its share sale has closed: about $93.5 billion of shares sold to the public at $83 each, plus $26 billion sold privately to partners such as Google, Microsoft and Nvidia. After a strong first day, the shares fell on Friday to $83.05, just five cents above the sale price, before recovering somewhat. Fortune links the fall to a wider slide in technology shares and worries about Nvidia. Read more and the background.
  • A security researcher planted traps in two million AI requests and found that some were read by people who should not have seen them. A security researcher at the company Dragos hid unique web addresses and fake passwords in about two million requests sent to AI services, so he would know if anyone looked. Some were opened: he reports break-ins at at least three AI providers and resellers reading customers’ requests, even where nothing was supposed to be kept. Separately, the AI router OpenRouter has warned customers that requests sent to models of the Chinese company MiniMax may have been read. The lesson: never paste passwords or truly private details into an AI chat. Read more and the background.
  • Cursor, a popular AI coding tool, tells US lawmakers it may stop using Chinese AI models. Cursor, a popular AI tool for writing software, has told two committees of the US House of Representatives that it is considering dropping Chinese AI models, which many companies use because they are free to download, citing geopolitical risk. The committees’ report, seen by CNBC, also recommends an American programme of free models and a ban on Chinese models in federal government systems. Cursor has not commented publicly. Read more and the background.

Also on the website today: Thinking Machines releases Inkling 2 Mini, a free model that runs on a laptop by going over its own work three times, Microsoft unveils seven AI models of its own, pitched as much cheaper than rivals, Study: America’s largest data centres emit almost as much carbon as Denmark.

Answer to the question of the day. To a large extent, yes, says an article from the Museum of Cryptography published in the Russian magazine Sistemny Blok. During the Second World War, the British codebreaking centre at Bletchley Park needed to read messages sent by the German high command on a cipher machine called Lorenz. A Cambridge mathematician, Bill Tutte, worked out how that machine was built without ever seeing one, from intercepted messages and a German operator’s mistake of reusing the same settings. To do the enormous number of comparisons needed every day, the engineer Tommy Flowers and his colleagues built Colossus, an electronic machine full of radio valves; it first ran in December 1943, and its decoded messages helped the planning of the Normandy landings in June 1944. Earlier, Polish mathematicians led by Marian Rejewski had used mathematics and special machines to break the better-known Enigma. The article’s point is that for decades afterwards computers were used mainly to break and analyse ciphers, not to encrypt anything, because they were huge and expensive; and that much of this history was forgotten because it stayed secret. Most of the ten Colossus machines were destroyed after the war, and the article notes that a method for exchanging secret keys, published in 1976, had been found earlier at Britain’s intelligence agency and was declassified only in 1997. The article dates from March 2024. Sistemny Blok (Museum of Cryptography blog), “The secret life of early computers” (March 2024) (article in Russian).
